footer.text: Diets and production from FAOSTAT Food Balance Sheets ({year}); emission intensities from HESTIA, FAOSTAT and published life-cycle studies; fish from FAO FishStat and published studies; farmland from FAOSTAT; deforestation from DeDuCE; transport and electricity from the SSP scenarios, Ember and the IEA; warming from FaIR. Land-use change is counted only as the change in forest clearing and as optional regrowth on freed land.

controls.shift: Animal foods moved to plant foods

basis.label: Kept equal
basis.hint: What the plant foods match: the protein, or the calories, of the animal foods they replace.

replacement.label: Replaced by
replacement.hint: Which plant foods take their place: today's mix of protein-rich plant foods, mostly legumes, or soy and oat drinks (half soybeans, half oats).

controls.rampEnd: All levers fully in place by

where.label: Where
where.hint: Everywhere, or only in high-income countries, where people eat the most animal foods.

controls.groupsHint: A food you set here keeps its own share. The other foods follow the main slider.
controls.rampHint: Every lever, the diet included, ramps up from today and is fully in place by this year.
controls.shiftHint: The share of animal foods (meat, dairy, eggs, fish) replaced by plant foods, reached in full by the year above. It cuts the methane and N₂O of farm animals and frees farmland.

groupHints.ruminantMeat: Cattle, sheep and goats belch methane and need the most land. Beef and lamb avoid the most warming of any animal food.
groupHints.pigMeat: Pigs belch little methane. Most of what pig meat avoids is the methane of their manure and the crops grown to feed them.
groupHints.poultryMeat: Chickens turn feed into meat efficiently, so poultry avoids little warming, mostly that of the crops grown to feed them.
groupHints.dairy: Dairy cows belch methane like beef cattle, but a litre of milk carries much less of it than a kilo of beef.
groupHints.eggs: Like poultry, eggs avoid little warming, mostly that of the crops grown to feed the hens.
groupHints.seafood: Wild fish emit almost only their boats' fuel, which counts with inputs, the default. With biological processes only (Other options), they emit almost nothing, and the plants that replace them can add a little warming. Fishing's harm to sea life is not counted. Counting the carbon that uncaught large fish sink to the deep ocean is an option (Other options), off by default. It is under 1% of seafood's emissions.

controls.horizonHint: The year the charts end at, and the year the summary and the figures beside each lever are read at.

levers.title: Levers
levers.intro: Every way to limit warming in Planetshift, listed under the cause of warming it acts on, with the biggest cause first. Within a cause, the groups that avoid the most in full come first. Each slider is the share adopted, reached in full by the year above.
levers.noData: Not available: this lever's data is not in this build.

options.title: Other options
options.intro: Each choice below has a default and an alternative. Switching shows how much the answer depends on it.

scope.label: Emissions counted
scope.hint: The farm with the making of the fertiliser and energy it uses, or its biological processes only. Wild fish add only the fuel their boats burn, which counts only with inputs.

feed.label: Feed shared out
feed.hint: How each feed crop is divided between cattle, pigs, poultry and others.

baseline.label: Farming's future without the levers
baseline.hint: Today's diet growing with population, or the SSP2 path for farm emissions.

location.label: Where production changes
location.hint: Producers keep their share of world output, or each country produces for its own diet.

temperature.label: Observed temperature
temperature.hint: Two records of global surface temperature since 1850.

climate.label: Climate response
climate.hint: FaIR model runs with an uncertainty range, or the published IPCC AR6 values.

ssp.label: Rest of the world's emissions
ssp.hint: The scenario for the emissions the levers do not change.

notes.fossilMethane: Methane leaked producing oil, gas and coal in each country in 2022, from CEDS: oil and gas wells, their venting and flaring, gas pipelines, and coal mines. It is where the fuel is produced, not where it is burnt. With the levers, it is that methane less the share the two leak levers remove: at 100%, 75% of oil and gas methane and 50% of coal mines'. The levers that burn less fuel cut the world's leaks too, but the map does not split that cut by country. The tooltip gives each part.
notes.water: Freshwater taken from rivers, lakes and aquifers to grow each country's crops, raise its animals and make the farm's inputs. It is each food's litres per tonne times its production. HESTIA gives the litres of the crops it covers. Poore & Nemecek (2018) give the rest. Animal products count the water used on the farm, not their concentrate feed, which is counted on the crops. Fish farms are left out. The litres per tonne do not change with the levers, so the water changes with production. Water does not change the warming. The tooltip gives the land equipped for irrigation.
notes.waterScarcity: Water use weighted by how scarce water is where it is used (AWARE 2.0), in litres-equivalent. It covers only the crops for which HESTIA has the country's own aggregation, so countries are not complete and cannot be compared on it. It is not added to the litres withdrawn.
notes.production: Where food is grown, not where it is eaten.
notes.emissions: Emissions on the farm from growing food and raising animals. CO₂e weighs methane and nitrous oxide over 100 years, for comparison only.
notes.land: Cropland harvested for the foods in the model and permanent pasture, as a share of each country's land area. That is how much of the land farming takes. Eating less meat frees pasture and the cropland that grows feed. The tooltip gives the hectares.
notes.change: Each country's output changes by the same share as world demand for each food. Exporters change along with the countries that buy from them.
notes.quality: Neighbouring countries can differ only because their figures come from different sources.
notes.deforestation: Forest cleared for crops and pasture in each country once the levers are fully in place, in hectares a year. The tooltip gives today's clearing, the change and the CO₂ it releases.
notes.landCo2: Each country's net CO₂ from all land-use change: forest cleared for any reason, peat drained and other changes, less forest regrowing on abandoned land. Blue countries take up more than they release. Today's figure is the mean of the Global Carbon Budget's three bookkeeping models over the years shown. The levers change two parts of it. One is the forest cleared for farming (the Deforestation layer shows its area). The other is the CO₂ that freed farmland takes up as it grows back, when Freed farmland is set to Grows back in the options. The rest of each country's land-use CO₂ stays as it is.
notes.mammals: Cattle, buffalo, sheep, goats, pigs, camels, llamas, horses, asses and mules as FAOSTAT counts them, times IPCC's typical live weight in each region, per km² of each country's land. Each herd grows or shrinks with the production of the food it gives. Animals kept for work stay. The summary sets the world's farmed mammals against its wild ones. The tooltip gives the tonnes.
notes.species: The species of plants, mammals, birds, reptiles and amphibians that each country's cropland and pasture commit to extinction worldwide. Each is Scherer et al. (2023)'s factor for the land, times the species described in each group. It is a loss committed over time if the land stays farmed. It is not the number of species lost by a given year. Land newly farmed commits more species, at the factor for the next hectare. Freed farmland gives species back only when Freed farmland is set to Grows back in the options. Per Mha of farmland divides each country's count by its cropland and pasture. It shows where a hectare commits the most species. The tooltip gives the farmland.

waste.food: Food lost from harvest up to shops, and wasted in shops, in restaurants and canteens, and at home, in tonnes a year. The levers Food wasted after shops and Losses before shops cut it, and a diet shift changes the food it is a share of. Waste after shops is UNEP's estimate of its edible part. Losses before shops are FAO's share of each food lost, applied to the food balance, and follow the country's production. The tooltip gives each stage. Losses are counted by fresh weight as harvested, so heavy, watery crops such as sugar cane weigh most, and the tonnes are higher than FAO's and UNEP's usual figures (see Methodology).
waste.municipal: The household and commercial waste each country's towns collect or should collect, in tonnes a year: the World Bank's estimate for 2022 from What a Waste 3.0. No lever changes it. The food levers cut food waste, but not the municipal waste shown here. The tooltip gives its largest types and where it goes. A country that reports neither takes its income group's shares.
waste.plastic: Plastic that reaches the ocean through rivers, in tonnes a year, from Meijer et al. (2021)'s model of the plastic that leaves each country's land by its rivers. No lever changes it. The estimates are uncertain: a river's true figure can be several times lower or higher.
waste.methane: The methane of landfills, open dumps and wastewater in each country, in kg a year, from CEDS for 2022. The Landfills and Wastewater levers cut it: gas captured at landfills, organic waste composted or digested, sewage treated. The levers that grow less food cut it too, as less food is wasted. A country's room to capture landfill gas is the share of its buried waste that goes to landfills rather than open dumps or is never collected (What a Waste 3.0). With the levers, the map shows the cut once the levers are in full and the waste already buried has rotted away. The tooltip shows landfills and wastewater separately.

oceanChart.title: Ocean pH
oceanChart.label: Surface ocean pH from 1850 to {year}: modelled and modelled with levers, with their ranges
oceanChart.caption: The pH of the surface ocean, from FaIR's CO₂ in the air and the chemistry of seawater. A lower pH is a more acidic ocean. Only the CO₂ the levers avoid changes the pH. Methane and air pollution do not. The observed line is the Copernicus Marine Service's global mean since 1985 (Generated using E.U. Copernicus Marine Service Information; doi:10.48670/moi-00224).

seaLevelChart.title: Sea-level rise
seaLevelChart.label: Sea-level rise to {year}: observed, modelled, and modelled with levers, with their likely ranges
seaLevelChart.caption: Global mean sea-level rise, from a rate of rise per °C fitted to the IPCC's projections (AR6), without the levers and with them. Each line is measured from the sea's level in 1900. The observed line shows tide gauges from 1900 (IPCC AR6), then NASA's satellites from 1993. The sea keeps rising for centuries. The gap keeps growing after 2100.

avoidedChart.title: Warming avoided
avoidedChart.label: Warming avoided by the levers each year to {year}, with its likely range
avoidedChart.caption: How much cooler the world is each year with the levers than without them. It grows as the levers ramp up. The warming of methane already avoided fades within decades.
avoidedChart.emptyHint: Move a lever or shift the diet in the panel.

chart.scenarioNote: The modelled lines follow the {scenario} emissions scenario.
chart.caption: The shaded bands are the 5–95% range of the climate response. Difference in {year}: {gap}.

summary.title: What the levers change
summary.gasYear: Once the levers are in full, in {year}
summary.landDetail: cropland {cropland}, pasture {pasture}; {share} of the world's farmland

seaLevel.label: Sea-level rise avoided by 2100
seaLevel.detail: Likely {low} to {high} cm. Without the levers, the sea is {baseline} m above its 1900 level by 2100 (likely {baselineLow} to {baselineHigh} m), from a rate fitted to IPCC AR6. The rise the levers avoid keeps growing after 2100. This figure leaves that out.

water.label: Freshwater withdrawn for farming
water.detail: a year, once the levers are in full: {change}. Litres per tonne come from HESTIA for the crops it covers and from Poore & Nemecek (2018) for the rest. Fish farms are left out. Water does not change the warming.

mammals.label: Farmed mammals to wild ones, by weight
mammals.detail: farmed {before} → {after} of live weight once the levers are in full; wild, on land and at sea, {wild} (Greenspoon et al. 2023)

species.label: Species committed to extinction by farmland
species.detail: {before} → {after} of the {described} described species of plants, mammals, birds, reptiles and amphibians. Freed farmland left as it is gives none back (Scherer et al. 2023)
species.detailRegrows: {before} → {after} of the {described} described species of plants, mammals, birds, reptiles and amphibians, once freed farmland has grown back (Scherer et al. 2023)

fish.label: Fish the fisheries target, against an unfished ocean
fish.detail: {before} → {after} of the {unfished} there would be without fishing, as the catch changes by {change} (Bianchi et al. 2021)

summary.scope: Farm emissions (wild fish only with inputs), the CO₂ of forest clearing as it changes, and the fossil CO₂ the energy levers cut. Food transport is left out.
summary.clipped: In {count} countries a cut reached the part of a crop or milk that is processed (into oil, sugar, butter…) and was stopped there. That part is cut on the processed food instead.

byFamily.title: Warming avoided in {year}, by lever group
byFamily.note: Each group's part is the mean of what it adds over every order the groups could be counted in, so no group is counted first. A group acting on several causes is split between them. The parts add up to the total.

link.scenario: With the levers chosen, the world would be {avoided} cooler in {year} than without them ({ssp}): {parts}.
link.intro: Most warming comes from burning fossil fuels. Farming adds to it in a different way, mostly through methane from cattle and rice paddies, and nitrous oxide from fertiliser and manure. These gases trap far more heat than CO₂ while they last.
link.attributionText: Each band is the warming from one cause, or, below zero, the cooling. After today, each band is what is left once the levers chosen act on its cause.
link.attributionCaption: Medians of FaIR runs on historical emissions by sector, then the chosen scenario after today. Each cause is the warming its emissions add. Air pollution cools: its particles reflect sunlight and brighten clouds. Land use's albedo change also cools: cleared land reflects more sunlight than forest. The energy, heating and industry levers also cut the air pollution of the fuel they no longer burn, so its cooling shrinks when they act. What the baseline adds to the scenario goes into the cause it belongs to: farm emissions that follow the population, the data centres' growth, ships' cleaner fuel, permafrost and the people on Earth. The gap between the scenario's temperature and the sum of the causes also goes into Other human emissions, so the stack meets the line without the levers.
link.attributionLabel: Stacked chart of warming by cause from {from} to {year}, with observed temperature
link.gasText: Each band is the warming from one cause's emissions of this gas. After today, each band is what is left once the levers chosen act on its cause. Air pollution, aviation's contrails, land use's albedo change and the natural factors are not greenhouse gases. They show under All gases only.
link.gasCaption: Medians of FaIR runs on historical emissions by sector, then the chosen scenario after today. Each cause is the warming its emissions of this gas add. The interactions and other minor sources are the rest of the gas's warming. Each band is measured from its own 1850–1900 average. A gas whose emissions were already growing then, such as methane, starts a little below zero.
link.gasAttributionLabel: Stacked chart of the warming from {gas} by cause from {from} to {year}
link.whyTitle: Why the gases are kept apart
link.whyMethane: Methane is short-lived: about half of it is gone within twelve years. Emit less of it and the warming it causes starts to fall within decades, which is why a change in what we eat shows up before 2050.
link.whyNitrous: Nitrous oxide lasts about a century, so less of it slows warming steadily rather than reversing it.
link.whyCo2: CO₂ stays for centuries. The warming it has caused stays too. Adding the gases up as CO₂e hides these differences, so Planetshift computes the temperature from each gas separately.
link.whyHfc: HFCs are the refrigerants in fridges, freezers and air conditioning. HFC-134a, the main one, lasts about 14 years and traps over a thousand times more heat than CO₂ per kilogram. The scenarios give HFCs for the world only. So all of their warming shows under other sources, where the food chain's refrigerants are counted.

milestones.title: Paris Agreement levels

p15.full: 1.5 °C: Paris Agreement, pursue efforts to limit

policies.full: Current policies by 2100 (UNEP, Climate Action Tracker, 2026): 2.7–2.8 °C
policies.caption: The band at the 2100 edge is where current policies lead: 2.7–2.8 °C (UNEP Emissions Gap Report and Climate Action Tracker, 2026).

milestones.caption: Dashed lines: the Paris Agreement's 1.5 °C (pursue efforts to limit) and 2 °C (stay well below). Dots mark the year each median reaches them. Warming levels are 20-year averages above 1850–1900, because single years swing about ±0.2 °C around the trend with El Niño and La Niña. So 2024, at 1.55 °C, does not cross 1.5 °C.
milestones.never: not reached before {end}, with or without the levers
milestones.peak: Peak warming with the levers: {value} in {year}.
milestones.peakRising: With the levers, warming is still rising in {year}: {value}.

impacts.title: What the warming means
impacts.intro: What the IPCC projects at the warming reached around {year}, averaged over 20 years. Between the levels of warming a source studied, values are interpolated linearly. Beyond them, the card says they were not assessed.
impacts.atLeastNote: Above {level}, the source gives no value. This impact only grows with warming, so the card shows at least its value at {level}.
impacts.note: The ranges in the (i) are the sources' own, not the range of the warming. Economic damages are left out. The sea-level rise avoided is in the summary, and the ocean's pH has its own chart.

wgi.title: Extremes, times as often as in 1850–1900 (IPCC AR6 WGI)

hot10.label: Heat extreme once in 10 years
hot10.note: How many times as often a day as hot as the hottest of a typical 10 years in 1850–1900 comes over land. This is the median of the CMIP6 models.
hot10.short: Once-in-10-year heat extremes, times as often

hot50.label: Heat extreme once in 50 years
hot50.note: How many times as often a day as hot as the hottest of a typical 50 years in 1850–1900 comes over land. This is the median of the CMIP6 models.
hot50.short: Once-in-50-year heat extremes, times as often

rain10.label: Heavy 1-day rain once in 10 years
rain10.note: How many times as often the heaviest one-day rain of a typical 10 years in 1850–1900 falls over land. This is the median of the CMIP6 models.

drought10.label: Farm and ecological drought once in 10 years, in drying regions
drought10.note: How many times as often a soil-moisture drought seen once in 10 years in 1850–1900 comes in the regions that are drying. This is the median of the CMIP6 models.
drought10.short: Droughts in drying regions, times as often

extinction.label: Land species at very high risk of extinction
extinction.note: The share of the tens of thousands of land species assessed that will likely face a very high risk of extinction (critically endangered, in IUCN terms). The IPCC gives a range, not a central value.
extinction.short: Land species at very high risk of extinction

coral.label: Coral reefs lost, further decline
coral.note: The further decline of warm-water coral reefs. The IPCC gives more than 99% at 2 °C, shown as 99–100%.

arctic.label: Summers with an ice-free Arctic, out of 100
arctic.note: Summers when the Arctic Ocean is free of sea ice: one a century at 1.5 °C, at least one a decade at 2 °C.

rangeInsects.label: Insects losing over half their range
rangeInsects.note: Of 105,000 species studied, the share of insects projected to lose over half of the range their climate allows.

rangePlants.label: Plants losing over half their range
rangePlants.note: Of 105,000 species studied, the share of plants projected to lose over half of the range their climate allows.

rangeVertebrates.label: Vertebrates losing over half their range
rangeVertebrates.note: Of 105,000 species studied, the share of vertebrates projected to lose over half of the range their climate allows.

fishery.label: Sea fish catch lost each year
fishery.note: The world's yearly marine fishery catch lost, in one global fishery model: about 1.5 million tonnes at 1.5 °C, more than 3 million tonnes at 2 °C.
fishery.short: Sea fish catch lost each year

heatwave.label: People exposed to severe heatwaves at least once every 5 years
heatwave.note: The share of the world's people exposed to severe heatwaves at least once every 5 years, from one study (Dosio et al. 2018), not from the IPCC. It uses the same population (SSP3) at both levels.

chart.title: What the chart shows
chart.text: The chart shows global warming since 1850: the observed temperature, then two paths to 2050 or 2100, without the levers and with the levers you set. The shaded band around each path is its likely range. The Warming avoided tab shows the gap between the two.

levers.title: How the levers work
levers.text: The Levers panel lists every lever under the cause of warming it acts on. Open a group and move a slider to set how much of a lever is adopted. The chart, the summary and the map change at once. The figure beside each group is the warming it would avoid alone, in full. Every setting is kept in the page address, so a link to it reopens the same settings.

causes.title: Where the causes are
causes.text: The Causes of warming tab, above the chart, splits the warming by cause (fossil fuels and industry, farming, land use and the others) and shows how much the levers remove from each. The Methodology page explains every step and its sources.

share.subtitle: The causes of global warming and the levers that limit it, with the warming each would avoid by 2050 and 2100.
share.alt: Planetshift: global temperature since 1850, without the levers and with every lever in full.
